item.title: Two hospitalized after shooting in Sunrise Manor, LVMPD says
item.description: Channel 13 is learning from the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department about an incident in Sunrise Manor that happened early Saturday morning.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
Channel 13 is learning from the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department about shooting in Sunrise Manor that happened early Saturday morning.

WATCH | Channel 13's footage of the scene Two hospitalized after shooting in Sunrise Manor, LVMPD says

According to LVMPD, officers responded around 2:07 a.m. to 4100 Walnut Star Lane after receiving reports of a shooting.

Two individuals have been hospitalized, with one in critical condition and the other with unknown injuries.

Details are limited at this time. This investigation is still ongoing.

item.title: Clark High School locked down for hours after shooting in nearby Las Vegas neighborhood
item.description: Clark High School was placed on lockdown for several hours Friday afternoon after a shooting in a neighborhood near the campus.
item.author: Malik Patterson
item.content:encoded:
Clark High School was placed on lockdown for several hours Friday afternoon after a shooting in a neighborhood near the campus, forcing a scheduled football game to be relocated to Durango High School as police investigated the scene.

Hundreds of people were set to enjoy a football game under the Friday night lights at Clark High School, but that game was relocated after the shooting. At the scene, roads were blocked off and dozens of police cars were parked for several hours.

WATCH| Clark High School locked down for hours after shooting in nearby Las Vegas neighborhood Shooting near Clark High School

According to Metro police, the shooting happened in a neighborhood near Arville Street and Pennwood Avenue. Police say no one was injured, no one has been taken into custody and the investigation is ongoing.

For one local teen who wanted to remain anonymous, it was more than just a shooting near his high school. It happened on the street where he lives.

"I came home running and I was shaking," the teen said. "I have sisters at home, and I came running to check up on them. My mom's at work, so I'm like the only person that only takes care of my sisters."

Eugenia Olivas, who lives nearby, said she didn't hear the gunshots, but she's concerned the shooting happened so close to a school.

"I hear crazy stuff like around here happening," Olivas said. "But like I never seen this much cops around here."

Police say the investigation is ongoing.

item.title: Man killed during attempted robbery at east Las Vegas business identified; three suspects sought
item.description: According to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, three men entered a second-floor business suite intending to commit a robbery when the employee was shot.
item.author: Alyssa Bethencourt
item.content:encoded:
Three suspects remain on the run after a man was shot and killed during an attempted robbery at a business in east Las Vegas Thursday.

Employees at the complex near Flamingo Road and Pecos Road identified the victim to Channel 13 as Reynaldo Rodis.

WATCH | Man killed during attempted robbery at east Las Vegas business identified; three suspects sought Man killed during attempted robbery at east Las Vegas business identified; three suspects sought

According to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, three men entered a second-floor business suite intending to commit a robbery. Police said an employee lunged at one of the suspects in an attempt to stop the robbery.

One of the employees attempted to stop that robbery by lunging after one of the individuals, causing that suspect to shoot our employee, Lt. Robert Price said.

WATCH | Lt. Price's full media briefing Employee killed during robbery attempt in east Las Vegas, LVMPD shares

Rodis also had ties to the Las Vegas boxing community. On Friday, a boxing organization shared a tribute to him on social media.

Channel 13 found business records listing Rodis as a director of Elevated Life Ministry. A notice posted outside the suite states that the organization transitioned into a private membership association called The Align Collective.

Other signs outside the suite describe a members-only club, with guests required to be accompanied by a member and a waiting period for new members.

Police have not said why the business was targeted.

Roxanna Estrada, who works elsewhere in the complex, said she saw officers and emergency crews rush into the building Thursday.

We saw cops kind of just rush in there. We saw the EMTs and the fire department, Estrada said.

Estrada also told Channel 13 that the same business had been targeted about two weeks earlier. Channel 13 has not independently confirmed that claim.

When Channel 13 returned Friday, the suite was locked and its lights were off. Detectives were also seen going door to door, speaking with people inside the complex.

Estrada said the shooting has left people who work nearby concerned about their safety.

We are worried especially because if they attack here, they can probably come back, she said.

As of Friday, Metro confirmed no arrests had been made. Investigators are still searching for the three suspects.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Crime Stoppers at 702-385-5555.

item.title: Former Las Vegas resident says clean up voter rolls
item.description: Jennifer had no idea she was still on the rolls in Nevada, and said that the states should be able to determine if someone has moved when they trade in their drivers license, which she did long ago.
item.author: Steve Sebelius
item.content:encoded:
Jennifer DeVivo moved away from Las Vegas in 1996.

She and her parents only lived here briefly, before returning to New York.

She got a new drivers license, registered to vote and says she votes in every election in the Empire State.

But unbeknownst to her, she was still listed on the voter rolls as an active voter in Nevada.

Election mail keeps showing up at the southeast Las Vegas house she used to live in, and not just political mailers, but official election mail, including registration cards, sample ballots and even official ballots.

The home's current owner, Russ Lorenzen, just tossed the mail and figured the county would eventually see that DeVivo, whose married name is Jennifer Randazzo, was not voting and remove her from the rolls.

But the mail kept coming. And after Lorenzen saw Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar on television talking about the security of Nevada's elections, he was fed up. He called Channel 13 to tell us about the situation.

WATCH | Former Las Vegas resident surprised to find out she's still on Nevada voter rolls Former Las Vegas resident says clean up voter rolls

After our story ran, we told county elections officials about Lorenzen's problem. But in June, he got another official mail ballot for Jennifer. The same thing happened this month, when a sample ballot and an official mail-in ballot for the November general election showed up.

The story got Aguilar's attention, and he personally called Lorenzen to discuss the problem, and encouraged him to formally notify Clark County officials of the situation.

Still on the rolls

Meanwhile, Jennifer had no idea she was still on the rolls in Nevada. A Channel 13 reporter reached out to her family members in New York, and she returned a call, after verifying a reporter's identity online.

She told us that, save for a few visits, she hasn't been to Las Vegas in nearly three decades.

"I was surprised because I knew that the election wasn't always, you know, like I heard it wasn't secure. And when I go to vote here [in New York], I don't even have to show my ID, which I always question, because how do you know it's me?" she said in a Zoom interview with Channel 13 Thursday. "And I didn't think I was part of the problem in another state."

Jennifer said the state's should be able to determine if someone has moved when they trade in their drivers license, which she did long ago.

Nevada is a member of the ERIC system, the Electronic Registration Information Center, in which states voluntarily cooperate to ensure people when people move or re-register, their former state is notified. A total of 27 states and Washington, D.C. are members of ERIC.

But back in 1996, ERIC didn't exist. (It was founded in 2012.) New York became a member in 2025, so if a person moved today, their information would be updated.

Jennifer's information, however, was not.

According to a county spokeswoman, election officials need a formal written notice that a person has moved away or died before they can start the process of removing them from the voter rolls.

That can happen if the post office returns a voter registration postcard as undeliverable, or if a resident writes "return to sender" on the outside of an official mail ballot. People can also file a discrepancy report with Clark County.

That can start the process of putting a person's name on the inactive voter list, and eventually they will be removed from the voter rolls during regular list maintenance. There are currently more than 400,000 voters listed as inactive in Nevada.

(You can check your voter registration information and make any necessary updates online at vote.NV.gov.)

Jennifer says there's obviously a problem.

"I would just tell them [elections officials] that there's a flaw in the system, and, you know, voter ID is a must, one. And two, they should clean up their act with the making sure that [there's] more accuracy in their elections, because if it's happening to me with my mail, who else is it happening to and it's not being recognized and brought to anybody's attention about it."

She also said she was glad Lorenzen brought the issue to the news. Someone less honest might try to use the ballot to vote in her name, she said. "Thank God Russ Lorenzen is honest enough to say, listen, she hasn't lived here. He could you know, be checking off who he wants and double voting for his party," she said.

Before counting a vote, however, officials match the signature on the outside of the mail ballot envelope with the one on file at the elections department. If they don't match, the ballot is set aside until the voter is contacted and confirms the vote. Elections materials including with each mail ballot warn that voting more than once in an election is a crime.

For his part, Lorenzen says he is returning the mail ballot to the county, writing "return to sender" and "not at this address" on the outside. That should start the process of getting Jennifer's name off the list of active voters, officials say.

For Jennifer, who learned this week she's registered to vote in a state that hasn't been her home for nearly 30 years, the solution should be more simple.

"Well, the truth of the matter today, we live in the age of technology, right? There has to be some better way for people to vote and for it to be more accurate," she said.

Do you have a question about Nevada politics? Ask Steve at Steve.Sebelius@ktnv.com, or by clicking on the link below.

item.title: Local economist says AI could create jobs as well as eliminate them
item.description: A local economist says artificial intelligence could create new jobs and opportunities, while Southwest Las Vegas businesses adapt to a changing economy
item.author: Shakeria Hawkins
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence is raising concerns about the future of work, but a local economist says the conversation should also focus on the jobs and opportunities new technology could create.

Jeremy Aguero, a principal analyst with Applied Analysis, says innovation could help move Nevadas economy forward as businesses and workers adapt to a changing economic landscape.

People are worried about the jobs its going to eliminate, Aguero said. Were not having a conversation about the jobs its going to create and the ways its pushing us forward.

WATCH | Local economist says AI could create jobs as well as eliminate them Can AI Create Jobs? Local Economist Weighs In

Aguero pointed to the internet as an example of how technological advances can create new types of work and change the way people live and do business.

We can spend two minutes thinking about all the jobs that wouldnt exist if the internet wasnt created, he said.

Nevada ranked fourth in job creation last year, according to information cited in the reporting. Aguero says innovation could bring further opportunities, though the broader economic impact of artificial intelligence remains an important question for workers and businesses.

For small businesses, adapting to change is nothing new. But as AI and other technologies evolve, owners face questions about how to remain competitive while maintaining the personal connections customers value.

Gayla Young, owner of Pipeline Malasadas, expanded her Hawaiian doughnut business from Honolulu to Las Vegas in 2024. She said the economy was different at the time and that Southwest Las Vegas was an appealing market because of its strong Hawaiian community.

Young said the areas local population helped make it a good fit for the business and its products.

She also emphasized the importance of adapting as conditions change.

I think in general change is always something you have to evolve with, right? Young said. Otherwise, if you dont change, youre gonna be left in the dust.

As artificial intelligence continues to develop, Agueros message is that the discussion should include not only the jobs technology may eliminate, but also the new opportunities it could bring.

item.title: No injuries reported after shots fired near Clark High School, police say
item.description: Clark High School is on lockdown Friday afternoon after a gunshot detection system picked up possible gunfire near the campus.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
Clark High School is on lockdown Friday afternoon after a gunshot detection system picked up possible gunfire near the campus.

A source within the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department tells Channel 13 that officers are setting up a perimeter in the area of Tara Avenue and Foot Street as they investigate.

Metro police say no injuries have been reported at this time.

We are also hearing from a teacher inside Clark High School who tells us they are in a classroom and safe.

The school's football team is scheduled to play Durango High School at 6 p.m. We're working to find out whether the lockdown will affect the game, but the school's coach tells us the start time could be pushed back.

Channel 13 crews are in the area gathering information and will share updates as we learn more.

item.title: Arizona joins Nevada's lawsuit over Colorado River water cuts
item.description: The Arizona Department of Water Resources announced on Friday that they are joining Nevada's lawsuit against the Federal Government over the new Colorado River cuts.
item.author: Adam Klepp
item.content:encoded:
Arizona is joining Nevada in a legal battle over the future of the Colorado River.

The Arizona Department of Water Resources announced on Friday that it has signed on to Nevada's lawsuit against the federal government over new Colorado River cuts.

The legal action comes after years of failed negotiations among seven Western states over how to divide the Colorado River's dwindling water supply.

In August, the federal government finalized a new operation plan that required Nevada, Arizona and California to reduce their water use, while imposing no mandatory reductions for the four "Upper Basin" states: Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico.

Why did Nevada decide to sue? Southern Nevada Water Authority manager explains: Nevada sues feds over Colorado River cuts: 'We weren't looking for a fight'

Officials in Nevada and now Arizona have argued that the Upper Basin states should also be required to contribute to conservation efforts mandated by the federal government. Nevada filed its lawsuit in August, challenging the process used to develop the new operating guidelines.

The Upper Basin states maintain that they already use less water when river flows decline and that their legal obligations differ from those of downstream states.

Arizonas decision to join our lawsuit is an important step in challenging a federal plan that unfairly burdens the Lower Basin and fails to require the Upper Basin to make meaningful reductions," Gov. Joe Lombardo wrote on Friday. "Nevada will not accept a framework that puts our water supply and the future of our communities at risk."

What does this mean for you?

The outcome will have significant consequences for millions of people who rely on Colorado River water.

The lawsuit argues the federal government's new rules could cut up to 71% of Nevada's Colorado River water supply, threatening the water security of more than 2.3 million residents in the Las Vegas valley. Meanwhile, Nevada has already reduced its Colorado River water consumption by more than 40% since 2002 even as the Las Vegas valley's population grew by 875,000 people.

While the federal government's new operating framework took effect October 1, reductions to Arizona's water deliveries are scheduled to begin January 1, 2027.

Even deeper cuts remain possible in subsequent years under the federal government's 10-year framework. The legal dispute adds another layer of uncertainty as Nevada and its neighboring states work to secure a long-term agreement governing one of the West's most important water sources.

Experts warn Colorado River system is heading toward water bankruptcy

item.title: Inspired by family, Las Vegas-born tequila brand honors its Mexican heritage
item.description: A Las Vegas entrepreneur is honoring his grandparents' legacy through a tequila brand inspired by family, sacrifice and Mexican heritage.
item.author: Alyssa Bethencourt
item.content:encoded:
For Cesar Rodriguez, the inspiration behind his Las Vegas-based tequila company goes far beyond the drink itself. It's about family, sacrifice and remembering the people who helped pave the way.

As Hispanic Heritage Month comes to a close, Rodriguez, founder of Abuelitos Tequila, is sharing the story behind a business inspired by the grandparents who helped raise him.

WATCH | Inspired by family, Las Vegas-born tequila brand honors its Mexican heritage Inspired by family, Las Vegas-born tequila brand honors its Mexican heritage

Some of Cesar's earliest memories include helping his grandfather sell socks on the streets of Tijuana and accompanying his grandmother and mother as they cleaned homes across the border in San Diego.

When Rodriguez was 19, he lost both grandparents just one month apart.

Their influence helped shape the philosophy behind Abuelitos: "Drink to Remember, Not to Forget."

"We like to celebrate with tequila but we also have to celebrate that every generation that comes after gets to dream a little bigger because of those who paved the way," Rodriguez said.

From family inspiration to a Las Vegas business

Rodriguez officially launched Abuelitos in June 2026, building a company based in Las Vegas with its tequila produced in Amatitn, Jalisco, Mexico.

The tequila is made using Blue Weber agave and traditional production methods.

According to the company, Abuelitos has expanded to more than 65 restaurants, bars and retail locations across Southern Nevada since its launch.

Its Reposado has also earned top honors at the Las Vegas Global Spirits Awards, including Best Reposado Tequila, Best Tequila and Best Agave Spirit in Show.

Honoring loved ones through Da de los Muertos

The theme of remembrance is also carrying into an upcoming Da de los Muertos celebration in Las Vegas.

Abuelitos is partnering with Todo Bien at The UnCommons from October 23 through November 1 for an event centered on honoring loved ones who have passed away.

item.title: Henderson unveils $70 million Sports and Social Complex, the valley's largest indoor sports facility
item.description: The Sports and Social Complex held its ribbon-cutting ceremony today, completing the $70 million, 180,000-square-foot facility that Henderson officials say is the largest sports complex in the valley.
item.author: Malik Patterson
item.content:encoded:
Henderson's largest indoor sports complex is now open. The Sports and Social Complex held its ribbon-cutting ceremony Thursday, completing the $70 million, 180,000-square-foot facility that Henderson officials say is the largest sports complex in the valley.

Nearly 18 months of anticipation led to the grand opening, drawing city leaders and local residents to the new facility. which we first told you about in 2024.

WATCH | Henderson's $70 million Sports and Social Complex opens to the public Henderson's $70 million Sports and Social Complex opens to the public

14-year-old Ryan Villanueva was among the Henderson locals who attended.

"I like bowling, and that they had it there so pretty excited," Villanueva said.

The complex also features two-story laser tag something Villanueva said he had not yet had a chance to check out.

Richard Naft lives a mile away from the Sports and Social Complex and stopped by the grand opening to take a first look.

"It's very big," Naft said. "To have a facility where you can just wander around and exercise at the same time that's really nice."

Kemper Sports, the company behind the project, donated $10 million to bring it to life. The city partnered with other donors, bringing in the final $60 million needed to complete the project.

During the ceremony, Kemper Sports CEO Steve Skinner said the company's investment is hope that the facility will bring more people to Henderson.

"I'm very confident given all the excitement and the community involvement how successful this will be," Skinner said.

Henderson Mayor Michelle Romero said the complex will create more active space for young people.

"Oftentimes you're here for one of your children, but but you have other children. This will give them something to do as well," Romero said.

The complex is open seven days a week and is hosting a taekwondo tournament this weekend.

item.title: Las Vegas taxpayers pay $20,000 after jail officer preached religious sermon to ICE protest detainees
item.description: A Las Vegas jail officer preached a sermon to ICE protest detainees. The city paid a $20,000 judgment, calling it a "compromise."
item.author: Darcy Spears
item.content:encoded:
Las Vegas taxpayers are footing the bill for yet another payout stemming from the June 2025 ICE protest in downtown Las Vegas this time, $20,000 to settle a claim against a city corrections officer accused of using religion to threaten and intimidate people held in jail.

Our previous reporting detailed Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department payouts to protesters totaling nearly half a million dollars. But this settlement involves the City of Las Vegas directly, not Metro police. It centers on City Corrections Officer Bernabe Ibarra, who is accused of preaching a six-minute religious sermon to detainees even after at least one tried to opt out.

Watch the Channel 13 investigation: Las Vegas pays $20,000 after officer preached to ICE protest detainees

Kathleen Cavalaro attended the protest that night carrying a sign that read "Love Thy Neighbor As Thyself." Body camera video shows how the sign became a shield against pepper balls 48 of them, according to court records fired by SWAT Officer Mark Eshe and then-Deputy Chief Bryan Peterson. Court records also say Peterson shot her in the back as she was following orders and walking away.

As officers moved to arrest her, Cavalaro can be heard on body camera video asking:

"You're shooting me? What am I under arrest for? Because I called you a fascist?"

She was zip-tied and arrested, then taken to the Las Vegas City Jail.

Federal lawsuit filed

Cavalaro later filed a federal lawsuit against LVMPD, the City of Las Vegas, Peterson, Eshe and Officer Joel Tomlinson. The suit accuses Tomlinson of falsifying the declaration of arrest by backdating the time and moving the location into the dispersal zone to "manufacture" probable cause for a "failure to disperse" arrest.

The city declined to prosecute. Her lawsuit says Tomlinson filed a second declaration that still contained false or misleading information, omitted Peterson's role, and conflicted with body camera video. No charges were filed after that, either.

Cavalaro cannot discuss that portion of her federal case because it remains pending. But she can speak to the part that was settled in her favor on Oct. 7.

Overcrowded cells and an unexpected sermon

"There were approximately 100 of us that were put in holding cells in rooms that were over capacity," Cavalaro said. "And they held us pretty close to the 24 hours that they could."

Despite a Las Vegas Municipal Court order requiring protesters to be released on their own recognizance, her lawsuit says the city kept her in custody at least nine more hours. Jail security video she obtained through her lawsuit shows what happened after she was finally moved from her cell.

"They released about 20 of us together, and they brought us down and sat us at the tables," Cavalaro said. "And that's when the correctional officer came in and started preaching a sermon to us, and brought in a jail chaplain and two church volunteers."

Her lawsuit accuses Ibarra of delivering the six-minute sermon even after she tried to opt out.

"I thought I made it pretty clear that I was uncomfortable and did not want to participate, but it happened anyway," Cavalaro said.

The jail footage has no audio, but it does show Ibarra delivering the sermon.

"It was very strange religious language to me, because it was a lot of, like, 'I rebuke you in the name of Jesus,'" Cavalaro said. "But the general message was that we had misbehaved, and Jesus would be disappointed in us, and that there is nothing we could do to change the system, that we should all go home and we should pray instead."

Implying the language of prayer is OK, but the language of protest is not.

"And that we were on a pathway of spending the rest of our life in prison if we continued to go to protests," Cavalaro said.

ACLU warns of First Amendment fallout

Nevada ACLU executive director Athar Haseebullah warned that protests are likely to increase, and that aggressive law enforcement responses risk putting agencies in unnecessary legal jeopardy.

"In some of these protests, local law enforcement is not the target of the protest, so by sort of responding in an incredibly aggressive way in a harmful way in a way that violates the First Amendment and violates civil liberties and civil rights more broadly," Haseebullah said, "they will unnecessarily make themselves a part of the story."

And part of Kathleen's federal lawsuit.

Watch the body camera footage obtained by Channel 13 in January as federal lawsuits challenge police tactics against protesters: Federal lawsuits challenge Las Vegas police tactics against protesters'Using Jesus as a weapon'

"I think that using Jesus as a weapon against people in custody is harmful," Cavalaro said. "Because if you're a Christian, it's taking something that is sacred and turning it into a tool of intimidation. And if you are not a religious person, it's imposing a religious message onto people who, at that moment, are under complete government control."

After accusing the city and Ibarra of weaponizing religion against detainees, Cavalaro received an offer of judgment. The city called it "not an admission of liability," but "an offer of compromise."

The payout was $20,000 of taxpayer money.

"It's just time for people to actually open up their eyes and see that there are no consequences, and it's costing them money," Cavalaro said. "So, whatever side you're on: if you believe police should be able to act however they want with no consequences, I think everyone agrees that at some point we should stop paying for this behavior."

The city has no policy addressing religious sermons delivered by corrections officers to inmates. An on-camera interview with city officials was requested, but the city declined and would not make Ibarra available. He remains employed as a city corrections officer.

item.title: 'The Foundry' promises to bring 1,000 affordable homes to downtown Las Vegas area
item.description: A massive new development in downtown Las Vegas is underway with the goal of making home ownership attainable for middle-income families in a traditionally disenfranchised area.
item.author: Mary Kielar
item.content:encoded:
The former site of the Cashman Center and Grant Sawyer State Office building will soon be home to hundreds of homes for families in the downtown Las Vegas area.

Find out more about plans for the future development: Groundbreaking kicks off new chapter for affordable home project in Downtown Las Vegas

On Thursday, Channel 13 senior reporter Mary Kielar went to the groundbreaking ceremony for The Foundry. Its a planned gated residential community with more than 1,000 townhomes and single-family homes spanning more than 70 acres.

This was the kickoff to let people know there will soon be a new place to put down roots in an area that hasnt always been desirable to all.

That includes Las Vegas Mayor Shelley Berkley.

We are reimagining this part of town, which I said in my earlier remarks, is a part of town that probably, my mother wouldnt let me go to on my own, she said.

But thats all about to change, Berkley told Channel 13.

This is going to be a beautiful neighborhood of solid, middle-income families that are raising their children in a clean and safe environment," she said.

It's also an effort close Ward 5 Councilwoman Shondra Summers-Armstrong's heart. Shell be representing the families who will eventually call The Foundry home.

What we are seeing is unaffordability all the way around in our community, and this will offer an opportunity for working folks, she said.

The hope is to have homes starting in the $300,000 range significantly lower than the average price in Las Vegas, which Redfin reports is around $450,000.

If you want to learn more, Lennar Corporations website is a good place to start. You can get on the list to show youre interested in joining the community. In about a month, developers tell us there will be a specific landing page for The Foundry.

Construction is set to begin on the homes there in October 2027.

item.title: Employee killed in attempted robbery in east Las Vegas, LVMPD shares
item.description: A homicide investigation is underway after a person was fatally shot in east Las Vegas on Thursday, October 15.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
UPDATE

Were learning more from Metro police about a homicide that took place this morning in east Las Vegas.

According to LVMPD, three male individuals entered a shared business complex with the intent to rob it.

An employee attempted to stop the robbery "by lunging at one of the individuals," and was shot by one of the suspects in the process.

No suspects are in custody at this time.

WATCH | LVMPD holds media briefing on this incident Employee killed during robbery attempt in east Las Vegas, LVMPD shares

ORIGINAL STORY

A homicide investigation is underway after police say a person was shot in east Las Vegas.

Police said they received reports at 11:40 a.m. of gunfire near a business in the 3400 block of East Flamingo Road, near Pecos Road.

Officers found a person suffering from a gunshot wound who was declared dead at the scene.

"This incident is currently under investigation, and LVMPD Homicide has been advised," a spokesperson for the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department stated.

This is a developing story. A Channel 13 crew is en route to the area.

item.title: Two critically injured in wrong-way crash on Sahara Ave., Tenaya Way
item.description: Las Vegas police are investigating a head-on collision at the intersection of Sahara Avenue and Tenaya Way on Thursday.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
UPDATE

We're learning more about a collision in west Las Vegas that critically injured two people on Thursday.

The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department shared with use that the incident was confirmed to be a wrong-way crash, which happened around 11:27 a.m. today.

Police determined that a Honda CR-V was driving eastbound in the westbound lanes on Sahara Avenue, "at a high rate of speed."

The Honda crashed into a BMW when "for unknown reasons," it moved right after the intersection.

A Hyundai and a Mercedes-Benz traveling behind the BMW were impacted by debris. Neither of those drivers sustained injuries as a result.

Five vehicles at a car dealership were also struck and damaged during the incident.

The drivers of the BMW and the Honda were both hospitalized in critical condition.

The Honda's driver, identified as 58-year-old Corazon Blackwell, was "booked in absentia at the Clark County Detention Center (CCDC) for reckless driving-related charges," LVMPD said.

ORIGINAL STORY

A west Las Vegas intersection is shut down on Thursday after a head-on collision between two vehicles.

The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department says the crash was reported at 11:27 a.m. near the intersection of Sahara Avenue and Tenaya Way.

One person was taken to an area hospital in unknown condition. Police said medical personnel were "still assisting" the occupant of the second vehicle.

The intersection has been shut down while police investigate. Members of the public were asked to avoid the area.

item.title: What we know about the body found in a barrel at Lake Mead in 2022
item.description: The homicide victim found inside a barrel that washed ashore at Hemenway Harbor is expected to be publicly identified Thursday. Here's a look back at how the case has unfolded.
item.author: Alyssa Roberts
item.content:encoded:
In May 2022, the waters of Lake Mead gave up a secret that has puzzled investigators for years until now.

The homicide victim found inside a barrel that washed ashore at Hemenway Harbor was publicly identified Thursday during a press conference with the Clark County Coroner's Office, Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, and forensic investigators.

DNA evidence helped identify the man as Edward Lelburian Jackson, of Arkansas. Investigators believe he was in his mid-to-late 50s when he died.

The discovery of Jackson's remains came as drought caused receding waters at Lake Mead to reveal several long-held secrets, including at least four sets of human remains. But the identity of the man in the barrel remained a mystery for more than four years.

Investigators released several clues over the years since, including photos of the man's clothing.

Here's a look back at how the case has unfolded.

May 1, 2022 National Park Service rangers report the discovery of a body in a barrel at Lake Mead's Hemenway Harbor.

May 2, 2022 After an initial autopsy, Las Vegas police say they believe the man was likely murdered in the mid-1970s to early 1980s. Thirty to 40 years earlier, police said, the water where the barrel was dropped would have been 50 to 60 feet deep.

Former LVMPD Lt. Ray Spencer shared updates on the investigation in May 2022: LVMPD says barrel dumped in Lake Mead containing remains was from 1980s

May 3, 2022 Police reveal that the man died from a gunshot wound, and that his death was likely a homicide.

June 2022 The unsolved case prompts speculation about possible mob connections. Former Las Vegas Mayor Oscar Goodman who represented many Las Vegas mobsters as a criminal defense attorney was asked about the case and remarked: We have no idea who's in the barrel at this point in time, and even if I knew who was in [there], I would not tell the good folks of Channel 13, because theyll end up in a barrel. The FBI also reveals it is assisting local law enforcement with the investigation.

November 2023 Composite images of the man found in the barrel, created by FBI investigators, are made public as investigators seek additional leads.

June 2024 As the investigation continues, photos of the man's clothing are posted on the National Missing and Unidentified Persons website. The pictures include a short-sleeved, button-down shirt, a pair of sneakers believed to have been sold at Kmart in the 1970s to 1990s, and a pair of pants that appear to be made of denim.

The case was the first of at least four bodies found at Lake Mead in the summer and early fall of 2022.

May 7, 2022 Paddleboarders discover skeletal remains in the Callville Bay area. The remains were since identified as 42-year-old Thomas Erndt, of Las Vegas, who reportedly drowned at Lake Mead 20 years earlier.

July 25, August 6 and August 16, 2022 Lake Mead visitors find human remains in the same general area, near the shoreline of Boulder Beach. Medical examiners determined the remains all belonged to the same person, since identified as Claude Russell Pensinger, of Las Vegas. Officials say Pensinger was 52 at the time of his disappearance on July 14, 1998. The cause of his death was undetermined.

October 17, 2022 Additional skeletal remains are discovered near Callville Bay. More remains found on October 19, 2022 are identified as belonging to the same person: 39-year-old Donald P. Smith, of North Las Vegas, who reportedly drowned at the lake in April 1974.

While Jackson's identity is finally known, investigators say their work isn't over and won't be until they identify who killed him.

Senior reporter Alyssa Bethencourt has more on new details revealed in the lengthy investigation: Mystery solved: Investigators identify body found in barrel at Lake Mead in 2022

item.title: Man in custody after reported knife assault leads to SWAT standoff in east Las Vegas
item.description: Las Vegas police say a man is in custody after a SWAT standoff in east Las Vegas that lasted nearly 10 hours on Thursday.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
Las Vegas police say a man is in custody after a SWAT standoff in east Las Vegas that lasted nearly 10 hours on Thursday.

Police said they were called to the area of Nellis Boulevard and Twain Avenue at 6:25 a.m. on reports that a man had assaulted someone with a knife.

When officers attempted to arrest the man, police say he barricaded himself inside an apartment in the 3800 block of South Nellis Boulevard.

As of 11 a.m., SWAT and crisis negotiators had been called in to assist. As of 4 p.m. Thursday, police said the man was in custody. They did not immediately release his name or any additional details about the investigation.

Members of the public had been asked to avoid the area while the standoff was ongoing.

item.title: First Friday on pause after deadly Arts District shooting; businesses support safety review
item.description: Organizers say the future of the longtime event is being reevaluated following a fatal shooting, while business owners call for stronger security measures before its return.
item.author: Shellye Leggett
item.content:encoded:
The future of Las Vegas' iconic First Friday event remains uncertain after a deadly shooting in the Arts District prompted organizers to put the monthly gathering on pause.

For 24 years, First Friday has drawn thousands of visitors to downtown Las Vegas for art, music, food and community celebrations. But organizers say the event needs time to reassess safety measures after gunfire erupted during the Oct. 2 event.

The shooting left a 15-year-old dead and two others injured. Police arrested a 17-year-old in connection with the shooting.

Witnesses described a chaotic scene as people scrambled for safety.

WATCH | Businesses support safety review after deadly First Friday shooting First Friday on Pause After Deadly Arts District Shooting; Businesses Support Safety Review Despite Economic Concerns

Kalani Heu, who works at Taverna Costero, said he was on the restaurant's rooftop when the gunfire began.

"I was actually working on the rooftop when it happened, so I heard the shots ring out," Heu said. "I did look over the balcony."In a statement to Channel 13, the First Friday Foundation called the shooting an "unacceptable tragedy" and said organizers remain "devastated and heartbroken."

The foundation said it plans to work with the City of Las Vegas, law enforcement and community partners to reimagine the event and determine what additional safety measures may be needed moving forward.

For businesses that depend on the monthly crowds, the pause raises concerns about lost revenue. Still, several business owners told Channel 13 they support taking time to address public safety.

"I put the safety of our staff and also the people that come in our store first before money," said Jimi Mastronardi of Star Las Vegas.

Others see the pause as an opportunity to strengthen the event.

"I think a reset is not a bad idea," said Chris Mahon of Taverna Costero. "Just kind of refigure it."

Business owners interviewed by Channel 13 suggested stronger perimeter controls, enhanced security measures and more comprehensive planning could help restore confidence among visitors and vendors.

Heu said while he does not want to see First Friday disappear, he understands why organizers feel a pause is necessary.

"I don't want to pause First Friday, but I understand the circumstances around it," he said.

The First Friday Foundation has not announced when the event will return. In a statement released Wednesday, organizers encouraged the community to continue supporting local artists while the Arts District recovers from the tragedy.

"As the community heals, we encourage everyone to continue supporting their local artists and one another during this extremely difficult time," the statement said.

Here is the foundation's full statement:

In light of the tragic events of this October, the production of the monthly First Friday event is pausing. We are taking time to work with the City of Las Vegas, law enforcement, and all necessary partners to reorganize and reimagine what the important future steps for First Friday can and should look like moving forward. We extend our deepest sympathies to the family of the young person who was killed and to everyone who was affected, and remain devastated and heartbroken over this unacceptable tragedy. We know that this has an impact on local artists, musicians, vendors, and local businesses, all of whom we are incredibly grateful to for bringing their unique gifts, talents, and services together to celebrate local creativity for the last 24 years, and for the light and positivity they have supplied in creating a vibrant and important local arts community. As the community heals, we additionally encourage everyone to continue supporting their local artists and one another in this extremely difficult time.

item.title: Man dead after shooting outside business in northeast Las Vegas; no suspects in custody
item.description: A man died after a shooting Wednesday evening in the parking lot of a business in the northeast valley, according to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
A man died after a shooting Wednesday evening in the parking lot of a business in the northeast valley, according to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department.

The shooting happened outside of Z's Supermarket in the 4700 block of East Owens Avenue near Marion Drive.

According to Lt. Robert Price with LVMPD, officers received a ShotSpotter notification around 7:30 p.m. followed by a 911 call reporting that someone had been shot.

When officers arrived at the scene, they located the victim, identified as a man in his late-20s, suffering from gunshot wounds. He was taken to the hospital, where he died.

Price said the victim was walking outside of the business while the suspects were walking toward the business.

"At some point in time, words were exchanged and a physical altercation ensued, resulting in the suspect pulling out a firearm and shooting our victim," Price said.

It is unknown what words were exchanged that led to the altercation. Price said the suspect fled the area in an SUV.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact the LVMPD Homicide Section by phone at 702-828-3521 or by email at homicide@lvmpd.com. To remain anonymous, you can contact Crime Stoppers by phone at 702-385-5555 or online HERE.

item.title: Clark County issues air quality dust advisory for Thursday; what to know
item.description: Clark County has shared with Channel 13 that high winds are projected to hit the valley on Oct. 15, prompting them to issue an air quality advisory.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
Clark County has shared with Channel 13 that high winds are projected to hit the valley on Oct. 15, prompting them to issue an air quality advisory.

From 8 a.m. to 11 a.m. on Thursday, wind gusts up to 40 mph are anticipated which may kick up airborne dust in the city.

According to Clark County, this dust can "[aggravate] respiratory diseases." With this in mind, those prone to being affected, such a children, older adults, and those with heart or lung disease are advised to remain indoors.

Wondering how you can control your dust exposure ahead of the advisory? Here's what the county recommends:

Limit outdoor exertion on windy days when dust is in the air. Keep windows and doors closed. Run your air conditioner inside your house and car to filter out particulates. Consider changing your indoor air filters if they are dirty. Dont take short cuts across vacant lots. To keep dust down, drive slowly on unpaved roads. Ride off-road vehicles in approved areas outside the urban Las Vegas Valley. Call Environment and Sustainabilitys dust complaint hotline at 702-385-DUST (3878) to report excessive amounts of blowing dust from construction sites, vacant lots or facilities.

To stay up-to-date with valley weather, visit ktnv.com/weather.

item.title: Las Vegas man sentenced to 5 years in prison for arson at Tesla collision center
item.description: A Las Vegas man was sentenced to five years in federal prison Wednesday after admitting to shooting vehicles and throwing Molotov cocktails at a Tesla collision center in the southwest valley in 2025.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
A Las Vegas man was sentenced to five years in federal prison Wednesday after admitting to shooting vehicles and throwing Molotov cocktails at a Tesla collision center in the southwest valley in 2025.

Paul Hyon Kim was sentenced to 60 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release. He must also pay over $227,000 in restitution.

Prosecutors had recommended a 20-year prison sentence, according to the U.S. Attorneys Office for the District of Nevada. The judge declined the terrorism enhancement of the charges, saying there was not enough evidence to prove intent.

According to court documents and statements made in court, Kim attacked the Tesla collision center on Badura Avenue near Jones Boulevard during the early morning hours of March 18, 2025.

Investigators said Kim used a .300 Blackout AR-platform semiautomatic rifle to shoot out two exterior security cameras before spray-painting the word RESIST on the facilitys entrance doors.

He then fired several shots into Tesla vehicles parked outside the repair facility and threw three Molotov cocktails into three vehicles, according to investigators. Two of the devices exploded and started fires, while the third did not detonate.

The attack left five vehicles destroyed beyond repair, authorities said. Kim fled on foot to his car and drove away.

Kim pleaded guilty in February to two counts of arson of property used in interstate commerce, one count of attempted arson of property used in interstate commerce and one count of unlawful possession of an unregistered firearm classified as a destructive device.

The Department of Justice has been clear: anyone who participates in domestic terrorism will suffer severe legal consequences, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada said. "There is no place for violence as a means of resolving political differences in our democracy."

Keeping our streets safe requires unified action across local, state and federal lines, Delzotto said.

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives also assisted with the investigation. ATF Special Agent in Charge John Wester said the agency deployed arson experts, including members of its Arson Task Force, a collaboration between ATF and the Clark County Fire Department.

Threats to public safety will be taken seriously, Wester said. Crimes of this nature will not be tolerated.

The FBI, ATF and the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department investigated the case, with significant assistance from the Clark County Fire Department.

item.title: Henderson mayor unveils homeless transition housing, affordable plans at state of the city address
item.description: Mayor Michelle Romero outlined new city projects today at the annual state of the city address, including a new homeless transition facility, a new preschool, and 1,000 units of attainable housing.
item.author: Malik Patterson
item.content:encoded:
Henderson mayor Michelle Romero outlined new city projects Wednesday at the annual state of the city address, including a new homeless transition facility, a new preschool, and 1,000 units of attainable housing.

The new homeless transition facility will be located at the Dignity Health Hospital off Lake Mead Highway. The facility is designed to help address homelessness and provide services for veterans.

"Addiction assistance or things like that, or getting into a home, training for a job, those types of things, getting them pointed in the right direction," Romero said.

WATCH | Henderson's plans from the State of the City address Henderson State of the City

The mayor also highlighted efforts to help veterans access essential documents.

"Veterans, for example, they might not be able to get a hold of their two DD 214. We help them get those documents," Romero said.

I spoke to Henderson residents about the changes they most want to see in their city. Homelessness and veteran rehabilitation ranked among the top priorities.

"We have a homeless problem. I think we need more shelters," Neveah Baker said.

"It's gonna take a lot of doing to get them get them to come in to get some help. Cause a lot of them got mental help because they've been the war," John Jamar said.

Henderson resident Isaac Proach shared what he values about the city.

"I love the park and public spaces," Proach said.

Proach also pointed to broader quality of life concerns.

"Housing costs, healthcare, gasses, gas prices, all that stuff," Proach said.

"Anything that will improve the quality of life of the common everyday people," Proach said.

On housing, Mayor Romero said new projects have already been approved or are under construction.

"1,000 units of attainable housing, either approved or under construction now, and many of our new projects also contain homes on the lower end of the affordability scale," Romero said.

Many of the city's projects from the homeless transition housing to the reimagined Boulder Highway Project are set to be completed by mid to late 2027.

item.title: First Friday pauses monthly downtown Las Vegas event after deadly shooting
item.description: Organizers of First Friday, the monthly art fair and block party in downtown Las Vegas, are putting the event on pause as they work with city officials, police and community partners on its future.
item.author: Abel Garcia
item.content:encoded:
First Friday organizers announced Wednesday they are pausing the monthly art fair and block party in downtown Las Vegas in the wake of a deadly shooting.

LIVE INTERVIEW: Downtown Hospitality Group representative responds to pause on First Friday events: First Friday events on hold after deadly shooting in Las Vegas

A 15-year-old was killed and two other people were injured on Friday, Oct. 2 when gunfire erupted near Main Street and Charleston Boulevard. A 17-year-old boy is now jailed in connection with the fatal shooting.

The First Friday Foundation, which puts on the event, said it will work with the City of Las Vegas, law enforcement and other partners to reorganize and reimagine First Friday's future. Its statement did not specify a return date, but a spokesperson tells Channel 13 the pause will last at least through the end of the year.

Organizers acknowledged the pause will affect local artists, musicians, vendors and businesses that have supported the event over its 24-year history. They encouraged the community to continue supporting local artists and one another.

The organization shared the following statement with Channel 13:

In light of the tragic events of this October, the production of the monthly First Friday event is pausing. We are taking time to work with the City of Las Vegas, law enforcement, and all necessary partners to reorganize and reimagine what the important future steps for First Friday can and should look like moving forward. We extend our deepest sympathies to the family of the young person who was killed and to everyone who was affected, and remain devastated and heartbroken over this unacceptable tragedy. We know that this has an impact on local artists, musicians, vendors, and local businesses, all of whom we are incredibly grateful to for bringing their unique gifts, talents, and services together to celebrate local creativity for the last 24 years, and for the light and positivity they have supplied in creating a vibrant and important local arts community. As the community heals, we additionally encourage everyone to continue supporting their local artists and one another in this extremely difficult time.

The news comes after City of Las Vegas Mayor Shelley Berkley indicated a possible pause on November's event amid ongoing discussions about future safety precautions.

In a separate statement on Wednesday, city officials acknowledged the impact of the pause on the community.

"The First Friday Foundation, Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the city of Las Vegas share a common goal around public safety," a city spokesperson wrote. "The 18B Las Vegas Arts District is a unique and authentic neighborhood that is an integral part of the fabric of our city. We are all committed to supporting the artists, businesses, residents and employees that make the district so special."

item.title: Federal appeals court hands down ruling on Clark County short-term rental process
item.description: Appellate court judges are seemingly siding with homeowners after hearing arguments on issues with Clark County’s short-term rental process.
item.author: Mary Kielar
item.content:encoded:
Appellate court judges are seemingly siding with homeowners after hearing arguments on issues with Clark Countys short-term rental process.

"The ruling is actually a great victory for us. It not only says that the injunction was right to be issued but it also affirms that people, homeowners have the right, the inherent right, to rent their property on a short-term basis," said Jackie Flores, a short-term rental host and founder of the Greater Las Vegas Short-Term Rental Association.

WATCH | Federal appeals court rules on Clark County short-term rental process Federal appeals court hands down ruling on Clark County short-term rental process

The county appealed a federal judges decision to put an injunction in place in December 2025. The injunction came after the Greater Las Vegas Short-Term Rental Association sued the county.

That judge determined the countys short-term rental licensing process was likely illegal. The decision pointed to slow application processing times and fines for homeowners looking to rent out their space through companies like Airbnb.

The appellate courts ruling says The portal for short-term rental licenses only opened for a single window between 2022 and 2023. Since then, Clark County has not accepted any applications for short-term rentals or finished processing the applications that it has received.

Appellate judges also said the District Courts decision to put an injunction in place was not a bad one, but its too broad.

They said it effectively authorizes anyone in the County to operate unlicensed short-term rentals, including nonparties and those who have never applied for a license. This goes beyond maintaining the status quo.

Court papers indicate Clark County officials may be willing to re-open their application portal if theres a more narrowly worded injunction imposed.

"The best thing would be to just open up the application process up immediately," said John Marshall, a co-host of short-term rental properties in Clark County.

Clark County Responded in a statement:

The County appreciates the Courts finding that the District Courts injunction was overly broad. In narrowing the injunction, the County will be able to enforce our laws against those short-term rentals which disrupt our communities and harm our quality of life. The remaining concerns raised by the Court are being addressed in an ordinance amending the Countys short-term rental law, which is scheduled to be introduced at the October 20th Board of County Commissioners meeting.

You can find the ordinance amendment proposal and the October 20 board meeting agenda here.

"There are a couple of good changes that theyre doing but there are several that are not as good and thats the problem with the county. They create more problems instead of fixing them," said Flores, who plans to be at the meeting.

The county already unanimously passed an ordinance amendment in August, trying to prevent platforms like Airbnb from accepting payments from guests wanting to stay in unlicensed short-term rentals in unincorporated Clark County.

item.title: Green Valley High School crowns a historic homecoming queen
item.description: Gigi Hutchison is the first Green Valley High School student with Down syndrome to win homecoming queen.
item.author: Alex Eschelman
item.content:encoded:
For the first time in Green Valley High School history, a student with Down syndrome won homecoming queen. Meet Green Valley High School's historic homecoming queen. Video courtesy KVIG Informative.

Im so happy my friends voted for me," Gigi Hutchison said.

Down syndrome only describes a fraction of who Hutchison is as a person.

Im in student council, cheer, dance class and GVTV news," Hutchison said.

The well-rounded senior started cheering her freshman year.

I just went to coach and said, 'Lets try something,'" Gigi's mother, Lori said. "'Even if she is a manager, lets do that.' She said, 'No, were going to try her out.' 

From that tryout on, Hutchison has brought one thing to every practice, pep rally and performance: Smiles, Gigi brings nothing but smiles," Green Valley cheer coach Bailey Murry said.

Hutchison's positive attitude inspires others at school, and online. Her Instagram, @dscantgetmedown, uplifts millions through her videos.

"My favorite part is the fight song," Hutchison said.

Hutchison and the fight song go hand-in-hand, both carrying a vivacious spirit that leaves a lasting impression.

Her hardworking mindset and attitude has also inspired me and our team," said Green Valley cheer captain and fellow homecoming queen, Kaia Earl.

Hutchison is proud to represent the Down syndrome community, dancing through life no matter the occasion.

I had some really good advice from some random person in a parking lot someday," Lori said. "They saw Gigi as a baby and they said, youre going to be on the best roller coaster of your life, and that cant be truer words. So when you see someone that loves to come to school, give high fives to every person in the hallway give a high five back and just except them, because all they want is friendship and love. 

Green Valley kicks off postseason play on Friday at home.

item.title: Authorities seek vehicle involved in hit-and-run that critically injured Las Vegas professor
item.description: Authorities are asking for the public's help in identifying a vehicle suspected of being involved in a hit-and-run crash that left a Las Vegas professor in critical condition last week.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
Authorities are asking for the public's help in identifying a vehicle suspected of being involved in a hit-and-run crash that left a Las Vegas professor in critical condition last week.

The crash happened Oct. 7 around 6:30 a.m. at West Tropicana Avenue and South El Capitan Way. The pedestrian was identified by family as Ernest Bavarsad, an astronomy professor at the College of Southern Nevada who also teaches science at a local high school.

The Nevada Highway Patrol said a vehicle struck Bavarsad on the side of the road before leaving the scene. He was taken to a local hospital in critical condition.

NHP provided pictures Wednesday of the suspected vehicle before the crash, describing it as a burgundy 2010-2018 Dodge Ram pickup truck with chrome trim and an extended cab. Investigators said the truck is missing its passenger-side exterior mirror.

Pictures can be seen below:

Drivers and nearby residents who spoke with KTNV said they have concerns about traffic safety along the busy stretch of road.

I cant say that I seen this particular truck, I seen several that resemble it, said Michael Brandon, a driver who regularly travels through the area.

Brandon also raised concerns about speeding and suggested measures to slow traffic.

I dont know if the police thought about installing bumpers here, on this particular street to slow people down because because theyre going 20/30 miles over the speed limit every time I come here and its dangerous, he said.

Nearby resident Cathleen England said she was disturbed by the drivers decision to leave.

Its shocking that they didnt stop and render aid, if you hit a human being you should stop and render aid, England said.

Anyone with information about the crash is asked to contact Nevada State Police Highway Patrol Southern Command Headquarters at 702-668-4100 or 702-668-5211.

Those who wish to remain anonymous can contact Nevada Crime Stoppers at 702-385-5555.

item.title: Mystery solved: Investigators identify body found in barrel at Lake Mead in 2022
item.description: The homicide victim whose remains were found in a barrel at Lake Mead in May 2022 has been identified as Edward Lelburian Jackson, originally from Arkansas.
item.author: KTNV Staff
item.content:encoded:
After more than four years of mystery and speculation, investigators have identified the homicide victim found in a barrel at Lake Mead in 2022.

A forensic investigation identified the man, who was killed in the 1980s, as Edward Lelburian Jackson.

Officials with the Clark County Coroner's Office and the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department made the identification during a news conference on Thursday afternoon.

Watch as Jackson's identity is revealed and investigators share new details of the murder case: [FULL PRESSER] Investigators identify man found murdered in barrel at Lake Mead

Jackson was originally from Arkansas and, as of Thursday, detectives have not been able to identify his connection to Las Vegas, Lt. Robert Price said. Investigators believe he was in his mid-to-late 50s at the time of his death.

His remains were found in a barrel at Hemenway Harbor on May 1, 2022. Drought and Lake Mead's receding water line exposed the barrel after it was submerged for nearly 40 years.

In the years since the discovery, investigators worked to identify him based on skeletal remains preserved inside the barrel.

An autopsy revealed Jackson died from a gunshot wound to the head. While we now know his name and additional details about his background, Price said the case won't be solved until investigators identify the person who killed him.

Investigators are asking the public to come forward with any information they might be able to share about Jackson. Based on Thursday's press conference, here's what we do know:

Jackson was originally from Arkansas but lived in the Los Angeles area with his wife in the early 1970s. His last known residence before moving to California was in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Once he moved to California, "we lose track of him," Price said. Family members recalled last seeing Jackson when he visited them in Arkansas in the early 1980s. Police say he had a "brief" criminal history in Salt Lake City, Utah that included aggravated arson and conspiracy to commit fraud.

Price also addressed speculation in the years since Jackson's body was found that his murder may have been connected to organized crime. Investigators "don't have any information to support those theories," he said.

item.title: Clark County early voting: Voting centers less likely to have a line on Day 1
item.description: We looked at which polling locations saw the smallest turnout on the first day of early voting in 2024. Here's what we found.
item.author: Justin Hinton
item.content:encoded:
Saturday, Oct. 17 marks the first day of early voting in Nevada for the 2026 Midterm Election.

For those who'd rather not wait in line, there are a few voting centers, historically speaking, that might be a good bet.

We looked at which polling locations saw the smallest turnout on the first day of early voting in 2024. Here's what we found:

Clark County early voting: Tracking 2024's least busy voting centers on Day 1

Cambridge Recreation Center is a good place to go if you find yourself on the east side of the Las Vegas valley. Only 481 people cast a ballot at that location on the first day of early voting.

If you're in the northwest or North Las Vegas, Craig Ranch Regional Park saw some of the smallest numbers for early voting turnout on Day 1. There, 886 people cast a ballot.

Over in the southwest valley, Mountain's Edge Regional Park saw 225 people cast a ballot at an event tent on the first day of early voting during the general election of 2024.

Mountain's Edge Regional Park and Craig Ranch Regional Park will be open from 9 am to 7 pm.

Cambridge Rec Center is open from 9 am to 6 pm.

There are also several new voting locations since the last general election.

If you're in the southwest, the IKEA parking lot has been added as a long-term voting center during early voting.

On the west side of the valley, Downtown Summerlin has been added.

Just go to the parking lot east of S. Pavilion Center Drive. You can enter on South Spruce Goose Street, south of Marketwalk Place.

In North Las Vegas, Skyview Multigenerational Center, which used to be the Skyview YMCA, is also a long-term voting center.

item.title: Student arrested after bringing gun on campus at Desert Oasis High School
item.description: The Clark County School District confirmed the arrest in an email from Desert Oasis High School Principal Ian Salzman.
item.author: Shakeria Hawkins
item.content:encoded:
A student was arrested Tuesday at a southwest Las Vegas high school for bringing a gun on campus, Channel 13 has learned.

The Clark County School District confirmed the arrest in an email from Desert Oasis High School Principal Ian Salzman.

Officials say CCSD police were "quickly contacted" after administrators found the gun, and the student was arrested.

Shakeria Hawkins shares the reaction from parents and students Student arrested after firearm recovered at Las Vegas area high school

"There were no direct threats to students or staff," Salzman stated.

Amber Anderson, a parent with two children attending Desert Oasis, told Channel 13 she learned about the incident through an email from the school around 4 p.m. Tuesday.

It's terrifying, Anderson said.

She said she was glad no one was harmed but questioned why a student would bring a firearm to school.

Im glad nothing was done with it, but why bring it here if theyre wasnt a plan? Anderson said.

A student who spoke to Channel 13 off camera described the incident as happening outside the school as students were leaving.

They tackled him, right before he got in school after school, the student said. I was a bit worried, because what if he made it in?"

Parents are being asked to remind their students about the CCSD Code of Conduct and to have conversations with their children about reporting concerning behavior to an adult.

"The consequences of violating the Code of Conduct can result in students facing disciplinary action, and parents will be involved if their child violates these expectations," Salzman stated. "Appropriate disciplinary action" will be taken for the student involved in this incident, he added.

A similar incident at Green Valley High School earlier this month prompted calls from parents for heightened safety measures, including the installation of metal detectors on campus.

Parents demand metal detectors after gun found at Green Valley High School: Parents demand metal detectors after gun found at Green Valley High School

CCSD's most recent firearms confiscation report shows two handguns have been confiscated on school property since the start of the school year. One of those was at Green Valley; the other was taken from a student at Marion B. Earl Elementary School. The Desert Oasis incident has not yet been included in the report.

In total, police have now confiscated at least 15 guns since July 8, both off and on school property. School police have also seized three BB or air guns on school campuses since Aug. 10, along with 12 knives.

Students are able to report concerns through CCSD's SafeVoice reporting system by calling 1-833-216-SAFE (7233) or online at safevoicenv.org.

item.title: Henderson DMV location to permanently close Wednesday
item.description: A new, 72,000 square-foot facility in Silverado Ranch will provide both Henderson and Donovan DMV services later this month
item.author: Anyssa Bohanan
item.content:encoded:
Wednesday marks the final day of operations at the Henderson DMV location.

The closure comes just days after the DMV's Donovan Street location also shut its doors last Friday. According to the Department of Motor Vehicles, both closures are driven by aging and outdated infrastructure.

WATCH | Henderson and Donovan Street DMV locations close to make way for largest facility in Nevada

Henderson DMV to close permanently Wednesday

The two locations will be replaced by a single, 72,000-square-foot facility in Silverado Ranch. The new building, now the largest DMV location in Nevada, will house both the DMV's main office and commercial driver's license operations.

DMV officials say the new facility is designed to better serve Southern Nevada's growing population. But for locals who rely on the Henderson location, the closure is already creating real disruptions.

RELATED | Locals react to upcoming closure of Henderson and North Las Vegas DMV locations

Cathy Stuart was at the Henderson DMV on Tuesday getting a driver's permit for her son. She said she made a point of going before Wednesday's closure and is glad she did.

"It would have changed the whole day with his work, my work; I would have taken time off," Stuart said. "We would have had to drive farther with the gas prices. Everything, it just all, you know, compiles, snowballs. It's sad because we live here, we work here, and why should we have to drive so far away just to get our business done?"

The Silverado Ranch location isn't set to open until Oct. 26, and appointments there are not yet available.

With two locations now closed and the new Silverado Ranch facility still nearly two weeks away from opening, the DMV recommends making appointments at the following locations for locals who need in-person services:

7170 N Decatur Blvd 8250 W Flamingo Rd 2621 E Sahara Ave 

The DMV also says that many services can be handled online. You can find additional resources and what you can do online on their website here.

item.title: NSHE launches ‘Eyes Open’ campaign to boost safety awareness on Nevada college campuses
item.description: NSHE is launching a new statewide safety initiative designed to encourage students, faculty and staff to recognize warning signs and report concerning behavior before issues escalate.
item.author: Shellye Leggett
item.content:encoded:
The Nevada System of Higher Education (NSHE) is launching a new statewide safety initiative designed to encourage students, faculty and staff to recognize warning signs and report concerning behavior before issues escalate.

The campaign, called Eyes Open, is being rolled out across public college campuses throughout Nevada, including UNLV. Officials said the effort is focused on increasing awareness and empowering members of campus communities to speak up when something seems concerning.

WATCH: NSHE launches Eyes Open campaign to boost safety awareness on Nevada college campuses NSHE Launches Eyes Open Campaign to Boost Safety Awareness on Nevada College Campuses

Keep their eyes open and report any suspicious behavior that may be happening around you, and if something feels off or needs to be raised as a concern, please speak up, said UNLV Police Chief Arnold Vasquez.

Students said campus safety remains top of mind, especially in the wake of recent events.

Everybody has it in the back of their head that something could always happen, one student said.

Under the Eyes Open program, reports are reviewed by trained assessment teams that evaluate each situation individually. Officials said the goal is not to label someone as a threat, but rather to identify potential risks early and connect individuals with appropriate resources and support when needed.

Dont stay silent. Thats the one message I recommend, to not stay silent, another student said.

The campaign follows the deadly Dec. 6, 2023, shooting at UNLV. Since then, higher education leaders have continued efforts to strengthen campus security through investments in surveillance cameras, emergency phones and access control systems.

Students said those improvements help provide reassurance.

It does make me feel better that they are looking out for our safety, a student said.

Education leaders stress that reporting a concern does not automatically mean disciplinary action or that someone is considered dangerous. Instead, it provides trained professionals an opportunity to assess the situation and determine whether additional support or intervention may be necessary.

Officials said campus safety is a shared responsibility and are encouraging everyone in the higher education community to learn the warning signs and report concerns when something feels wrong.

item.title: 'Money maxxing': How families can make every dollar work harder as costs rise
item.description: With everyday costs on the rise, a viral trend called “money maxxing” is helping families rethink how they spend, save and make every dollar work harder.
item.author: Tricia Kean
item.content:encoded:
With the cost of everyday essentials putting pressure on household budgets, families are looking for new ways to make the money they already earn go further.

One approach gaining attention on social media is called money maxxing.

The term puts a new spin on traditional personal finance strategies. The basic idea is to make every dollar work as efficiently as possible, whether that means spending more strategically, taking advantage of available rewards or finding ways to build assets, without necessarily relying on a bigger paycheck.

For moms managing the day-to-day expenses of a household, local mom and podcaster Elli Ezra says the conversation needs to go beyond simply telling families to budget.

I think it's hard to tell mothers to budget. Gas is gas, groceries is groceries, Ezra said. So what I like to talk about is to spend smart and to acquire assets.

Ezra said spending smart can include taking advantage of tools that are already available to consumers, including credit card or debit card rewards.

Her message also focuses on taking some of the guilt out of conversations about money, especially when families are confronting expenses they cannot simply eliminate.

I think sort of taking shame and guilt away, things are expensive, Ezra said. It's not just about get out of debt. That's not what the wealthy do. That's not how they think. They leverage their assets to help them, and that is what I try to bring to the table with Mom's Money Talk.

Making your household finances work smarter

While money maxxing may be a newer social media term, many of the ideas behind it are familiar: paying closer attention to where money goes, looking for ways to get more value from necessary spending and thinking about finances beyond simply cutting expenses.

For families already feeling squeezed, the appeal is straightforward: Instead of focusing only on what they have to give up, the strategy encourages them to look at how they can use the money and financial tools they already have more effectively.

Ezra shares more of her approach to becoming the chief financial officer of your household through her podcast, Mom's Money Talk. She can also be found on Instagram at @momsmoneypod.
